title: Female reproductive anatomy: structures and functions
intro: Understanding reproductive anatomy can help describe symptoms, discuss sexual health and make informed choices. Bodies vary naturally, and a person’s organs do not determine their worth or identity. Anatomy information is not a test of sexual experience or fertility.

sections.heading: External structures
paragraphs: The vulva includes the labia and clitoral structures around the vaginal opening. The urethral opening carries urine and is separate from the vagina. Shape and size vary; comparison with edited images cannot establish what is healthy.

sections.heading: Internal structures
paragraphs: The vagina connects the external opening to the cervix, the lower part of the uterus. The uterus can support pregnancy; fallopian tubes connect toward the ovaries. The ovaries contain eggs and produce hormones, although anatomy can differ after surgery or through development.

sections.heading: Cycles and reproduction
paragraphs: Hormonal signals influence egg maturation and changes in the uterine lining. Ovulation and bleeding patterns vary and can change with pregnancy, breastfeeding, contraception or menopause. A regular-looking bleed does not prove ovulation or rule out every reproductive problem.

sections.heading: Comfort and care
paragraphs: Sexual pleasure involves nerves, blood flow, context and communication; penetration is not the only form of sexual activity. Consent and comfort matter throughout care and relationships. Gentle external cleaning is usually enough; internal cleansing products can irritate.

sections.heading: When to seek assessment
paragraphs: Persistent itching, unusual bleeding, a new lump or pelvic pain deserves review. Severe pain with possible pregnancy, fainting or heavy bleeding needs urgent help. Do not use the appearance of the hymen to judge sexual history; it cannot reliably establish it.
